1	# Task 11: Solar-system explorer with focus on click
2	
3	Build a single-page browser app with the provided framework, served by vite, rendering to the canvas with id #app. The app is an interactive, stylised solar system explorer on a dark starfield background.
4	
5	Show a glowing central star and at least 6 planets, each at a different orbital distance, with a different size and colour and orbiting the star at a different speed (inner planets faster). At least one planet has a moon orbiting it, and at least one planet has a ring. Draw a thin circular orbit line for each planet. Planets should also spin about their own axis. Use a simple procedural look (colour, gradients or generated textures); do not load external assets from the network.
6	
7	The user can click a planet to focus on it. On focus, the camera smoothly moves (about 1.5 seconds, eased) to a close view of that planet and keeps following it as it orbits, and a DOM info panel appears showing the planet's name, its orbital period in Earth days, and its distance from the star in million km. Clicking empty space, or pressing the Escape key, smoothly returns to the overview showing the whole system and hides the panel. In the overview, the user can drag to orbit the camera around the system and scroll to zoom within sensible limits. Add a toggle button labelled 'Pause' that stops and resumes orbital motion, and shows 'Play' while paused.
8	
9	The scene must look correct on first load with no console errors. Expose

content.thinking:
Since the camera controller's interface is unclear, I'm considering an alternative: instead of moving the camera, I could move the entire world in a root group with the camera fixed, inversely translating and rotating it to simulate camera motion.

To keep rotation math predictable without knowing the Euler order used by setRotation, I'll nest separate pitch and yaw groups (each rotating about a single axis) rather than combining both into one rotation call, with a pan/translation group inside for positioning.

The camera itself stays fixed at the origin looking down -z, so distance/zoom is handled by moving the outermost group back along z rather than moving the camera. That way world transform composes cleanly as translate-by-distance, then pitch, then yaw, then pan-to-focus, then the scene content.

For lighting, I'm uncertain whether a point light nested inside a group inherits the parent transform, since the documented recipes usually keep lights at the top level. As a safer fallback I'll lean on ambient/hemisphere lighting plus an emissive star so planets stay visible regardless, while still trying a point light at the star's position with large distance and zero decay in case it does follow the group -- if it doesn't, having it effectively at the camera gives a headlight effect, which is an acceptable fallback either way.

Since I can't actually verify behavior without the dependency available, I'll do my best engineering effort using only documented APIs for world transforms and position/rotation setters, and clearly flag the result as unverified in my final report. For planets I'll track each one's position and spin in my own state and update them per frame via setPosition and setRotation, with moons offset from their planet's position and rings following along as separate nodes tied to the planet.

Trying to figure out rings is tricky since I don't know the exact torus or ring primitive parameters—whether a flattened torus or disc shape will actually render a visible ring without the planet poking through or looking wrong.

I'll settle on using a few concentric thin tori for a banded ring effect, tilted with a simple rotation while keeping position updates separate, and reuse the same thin-torus trick for drawing orbit paths.

Switching to small box instances arranged along each orbit circle instead, oriented tangentially to approximate a thin line—cheap, reliable, and reads well at low resolution. Working out the rotation math so each box aligns tangent to the circle at its position.

Switching to spheres solves the rotation issue—small spheres spaced closely will read as a continuous circular line regardless of orientation convention, so I'm sizing them at 0.25 diameter with 0.5 spacing and scaling count by orbit radius for roughly 4000 total instances, using a muted emissive gray material, then setting up the planet scale distances.

I'm defining the eight planets with real names and stylized but proportionally increasing scene distances, picking a sun radius and default camera distance/pitch that keeps the outermost orbit comfortably in frame, and now working out individual planet sizes starting from Mercury.

For orbital motion, since real periods range too wildly (Mercury 88 days vs Neptune 60,000+), I'm compressing them onto a shared simulated timescale so all planets visibly rotate at reasonable relative speeds rather than Neptune appearing frozen.

I'll give Earth one moon and Jupiter two (Io and Europa) for simplicity, updating their orbital positions each frame.

For visuals I'll keep things straightforward with PBR materials and basic colors rather than risky custom shaders or unknown presets for banded planets like Jupiter and Saturn. The star gets an emissive sphere material for its glow.

I'll stick to the fields I trust rather than guessing at unverified ones, since the build won't typecheck but runtime should just ignore unknowns anyway. For the starfield, I'm planning around 600 tiny spheres on a distant shell, placed in a group tied to rotation (yaw/pitch) but not to the pan translation, so stars stay fixed on the sky without parallax drift.

Setting up a separate pitch/yaw rig for the stars so camera rotation stays consistent without the root's translation affecting their distance, keeping star color simple with an unlit emissive white material.

I'm checking that star size reads as a visible point rather than a sub-pixel dot given the distance and field of view, deciding to bump radius to 3-5 for visibility, and setting a dark navy background with a fixed origin camera looking down -z at 45° fov, while noting tone mapping could dim the emissive glow slightly but that's acceptable.

For picking I need to derive NDC coordinates from the canvas's bounding rect and aspect ratio, then work out the camera transform math: rotating content points by pitch and yaw using standard right-handed rotation matrices, pivoting around a focus point and pulling back by the orbit distance. I'm assuming three.js-style rotation conventions since I can't verify the engine's actual sign conventions, which carries some risk of mismatched drag directions during picking, so I want dragging right to correspond to increasing yaw so the scene rotates appropriately.

Working through pitch, I confirm that increasing the angle tilts the top of the scene toward the viewer, matching a camera looking down from above, with pitch defaulting around 0.55 radians and clamped between roughly 0.1 and 1.45. For focusing on a planet, I set the pan target to the planet's lerped position and adjust the orbit distance accordingly.

I'm planning the camera distance as scaled by planet radius plus a fixed offset, and setting up a 1.5-second easing transition where yaw, pitch, distance, and focus point interpolate from the starting snapshot to a continuously recomputed target (since the planet moves) using easeInOutCubic, locking onto the planet once the transition completes. For the overview state I keep the pan at origin with the user's last saved yaw/pitch, while for focus mode I preserve yaw but ease pitch toward a flatter angle around 0.3.

Dragging and wheel input should be limited to the overview state and disabled once focused on a planet. For computing the camera's distance to the focused planet, I'm deriving the camera's world position by inverting the yaw/pitch rotation applied to the offset vector along the view axis, then taking the distance between that position and the planet's position.

Unfocusing clears the focus state immediately while easing the camera back over 1.5 seconds, hiding the info panel right away. For planet picking, I'm casting a ray from the camera through the normalized pointer coordinates into camera space, then testing it against each planet's sphere using their transformed positions.

Since tiny planets like Mercury can shrink to just a few pixels on screen at overview distances, I need to pad the hit area in screen space -- projecting each planet's center and radius to pixels, then counting it as a hit if the click falls within the larger of its projected radius or a minimum threshold like 9px, picking the nearest match among overlapping candidates.

Clicking on the Sun or empty space should just unfocus since it's not a planet. For distinguishing drags from clicks, I'll track the pointerdown position and only register a click if the pointer moved less than 4px before release, listening on the canvas and checking whether #app in index.html is actually the canvas element.

content.thinking:
I'm positioning the pause button and info panel as absolute-positioned overlays at the canvas's top-left and top-right corners, calculating the panel's left offset from the canvas width.

Making the panel pointer-events-none so it doesn't block canvas clicks, and confirming the engine doesn't attach conflicting pointer handlers. For time handling, simulation time advances by clamped delta only while unpaused, with orbital and spin angles tied to simT, while camera easing keeps running on real time even when paused.

For __TASK_STATE__, I'm exposing a frozen, read-only object with getters that return fresh snapshots of planet positions in world/content coordinates, plus a ready flag set once the app finishes initializing.

I'm setting __EVAL_READY__ after the first real frame renders, waiting on app.ready() and then a couple of animation frames to be safe, and making sure initial planet positions are computed up front using the same function the update loop uses so the first frame is already consistent before any rotation is applied at runtime.

I'm chaining position and rotation methods onto the group builder for pitch/yaw/pan nodes, then marking them mutable at runtime so I can update them each frame; I'm laying out node ids for the sun, planets, moons, rings, and star layers, and setting up a point light at the sun's position inside the pan group.

For the light itself, I want it to stay correctly attached to the sun as the scene rotates, so keeping it inside the pan group makes more sense than placing it outside near the camera. I'm weighing decay and distance settings versus intensity to get believable falloff, since infinite distance with zero decay behaves differently than a realistic physical light.

I'll also add a dim hemisphere fill light using camera-relative axes, and set the sun's intensity and decay experimentally since exact calibration isn't guaranteed—going with a bright intensity, zero decay, rough PBR materials, and a neutral environment fill so nothing renders pure black.

Now I'm adding a bloom effect with moderate intensity and threshold, plus designing the ring torus material (tan PBR color, rough finish) and working out the torus geometry scale—mapping major/tube radius through the size parameters to get the right flattened, ring-like proportions without it looking too fat.

For bands I'm using two tori at different radii with different colors, scaling the y-axis down to flatten the tube into a thin ring shape, then tilting the whole ring by rotating around the x-axis.

Rings stay separate nodes that follow the planet's position but don't spin with it. For planet spin to actually look like something, a uniform-color sphere won't cut it, so I'm weighing options like a custom GLSL fragment shader that bands colors based on object-space position — though that risks compile errors — versus simpler tricks like adding a small flattened "spot" sphere as a child to visually indicate rotation.

Writing the shader code...

I'm weighing custom shaders against a safer PBR fallback, since black planets from a silent shader failure would be worse than plain coloring, and the task only calls for a simple procedural look anyway. For visible spin and texture, I'm leaning toward making each planet a small group with the main sphere plus a couple of darker, flattened "spot" children placed near the surface to act as cheap surface features.

Working out spot placement now: four spots per planet at deterministic angular positions, sized at roughly half the planet's radius and embedded slightly below the surface so they protrude as visible caps, giving the illusion of continents or markings without real texturing.

For the info panel, I'm setting real orbital data for all eight planets—period in Earth days and distance from the sun in millions of km—plus laying out scaled orbit radii and planet sizes for the scene itself.

Now I'm working out Saturn's ring geometry so it doesn't collide with neighboring orbits, and adding moons: Earth's moon with its own orbit radius and period, plus Jupiter's Io and Europa, keeping their positions roughly in-plane.

Now I'm figuring out the focus-camera distance formula so it scales with each planet's radius, checking that Saturn's rings and Jupiter's moons stay in view, and adjusting the camera pitch and yaw so the sun lights the focused planet appropriately.

For continuity I need to unwrap the target yaw relative to the current yaw so the camera doesn't spin the wrong way, then lerp smoothly during the transition while letting the target keep tracking the planet's orbit so it locks in correctly at the end. When returning to the overview, I'll similarly unwrap the target against the user's overview yaw value.

For the actual transition, I'm capturing the current live camera state the moment the focus changes, then easing from that snapshot toward the moving target over about 1.5 seconds using accumulated simulation time rather than wall-clock time, so it stays consistent even if headless tests use fake timers. If the focus changes again mid-transition, I just reset the "from" state to whatever the live camera currently is, which keeps things smooth. For the overview mode itself, dragging just updates the overview yaw/pitch directly, and the scroll wheel adjusts zoom distance multiplicatively within a clamped range.

Now I'm handling wheel events only when nothing is focused, with a non-passive listener so I can prevent default scrolling; the pause button toggles its label between Pause and Play, and Escape clears focus via the window keydown handler. For programmatic focus/unfocus calls, I'm matching planet names case-insensitively and treating them the same as a canvas click or click on empty space, while exposing the current focused state and distance-to-focus as queryable values, with an info panel that's hidden by default. For picking, I'm converting pointer coordinates into normalized device space and projecting each planet into camera space to determine what was clicked.

For hit-testing I'm computing the pixel distance between the cursor and each projected planet, picking whichever is closest in depth among plausible hits since occlusion by other bodies isn't handled precisely, and moons aren't included as clickable targets. For the per-frame camera rig, I'm setting the root, pitch, and yaw nodes' transforms so the world transform matches the pitch-then-yaw-then-pan hierarchy, and mirroring that same pitch/yaw setup for the nested star rig. I'm also positioning the light by transforming the sun's origin into camera space.

Now I'm setting up runtime-mutable IDs on the planet, moon, and ring groups (which live inside the pan group using content-space coordinates), adding a transparent glow shell around the sun, and building a small typed helper function for constructing groups with position options. For the starfield, I'm generating around 700 instances scattered on a large sphere, each sized and colored like a star, using emissive materials—though I'm second-guessing whether the emissive color actually gets multiplied by the per-instance color.

I'm deciding bloom will handle star glow so I can keep the star sizes small, skip fog, and move on to writing the orbit-line instances: one instanced sphere node per planet tracing out its circular path, with transform counts scaled to each orbit's circumference, totaling around 5500 instances combined into a single node with a soft blue emissive tint. Now I'm starting to write the planet group constructor function that builds each planet's sphere body with its own PBR material.

Writing planet group builder...

I'm checking whether the group builder supports chaining `.position()` then `.runtime()` the way other node types do, and sketching the surface spot placement using directional offsets scaled by radius. For spin, I'm setting each planet's rotation from a per-body spin rate multiplied by simulation time, accounting for retrograde cases like Venus. Then I write a coordinate transform function that converts a world position into camera space by subtracting the focus point, applying yaw and pitch rotations, and offsetting by the camera distance.

I'm storing each planet's position in a mutable array computed from orbital phase and angular speed, with starting phases assigned per planet. For the overview camera, I'm picking yaw, pitch, and distance values and checking that Neptune's orbit stays within the visible frustum at that distance, settling on a distance around 150 with zoom bounds between 50 and 300. Now I'm thinking through the transition interpolation field and starting to write pointer event handlers for drag-based camera control.

Pointer capture is guarded by try in case the browser doesn't support it, and I'm distinguishing a click from a drag based on movement distance — clicking on empty space unfocuses, clicking a planet focuses it, while dragging during a transition is still allowed. For easing I'm using an easeInOutCubic curve, and I'm writing a function that computes the target view: when focused, it derives yaw/pitch/radius from the planet's position, unwrapping the angle relative to the starting yaw during an active transition so the camera doesn't spin the wrong way.

I decide to always reference the "from" yaw while the transition is in progress, then switch to referencing the live yaw once it's finished, implemented as a simple conditional based on transition progress. Now I'm laying out the pause button and info panel styles — absolute positioning, dark translucent background, padding, pointer-events disabled on the panel, with distinct IDs for the panel and button, and making sure clicking the pause button toggles paused state and blurs focus without interfering with the Escape key.

I'm setting up the ready-state flag, exposed on window with getters, to flip true after the first frame renders, and sketching out the global typings for it. For node handles, I'll lazily require them by ID each frame and cache them in a Map rather than resolving them all upfront, since that matches how the runtime API is documented and the per-frame cost is negligible.
